name: water-tile
description: Procedurally paint a 16x16 water tile that is seamless side-to-side, then build a VERTICAL toroidal-shift flow loop so the wave bands visibly drift downward. The trick: every row is uniform across x, so the horizontal wrap seam is zero by construction (the tile still tiles left<->right perfectly) while a vertical shift moves real content between rows -- the frames genuinely differ and the GIF actually animates. The loop is five frames (dy 0,4,8,12,16) where the closing frame's +16 shift is the identity, so it lands pixel-perfect back on the start and the cycle closes. A worked example of how shifting along the seamless axis keeps the seam clean AND produces visible motion, with the seam/diff/loop audits proving both.

steps.note: A 16x16 canvas. 16 is a multiple of the 4px-per-frame flow step, so the loop advances dy 0,4,8,12,16 in five even quarter-steps and the last one (12 + 4 = 16 == 0 by toroidal wrap) lands pixel-perfect back on the start. The cycle closes onto itself with no remainder.

A vertical 3-stop blue depth ramp: lighter water near the top, mid water, deep shadow at the bottom -- the read of looking down through water. The axis is purely vertical (x0 == x1) and dither is 'none', so the lerp paints each ROW a single solid colour across all 16 columns. Because every row is constant in x, column 15 equals column 0 on every row -- that is exactly what makes the tile seamless left<->right. (An ordered 'bayer' dither would look richer but its 4px phase pattern makes column 15 differ from column 0, reintroducing a hairline horizontal seam on a 16-wide tile; we keep dither 'none' to guarantee the clean horizontal seam.)

Three full-width horizontal wave bands in lighter tones: a bright two-row crest (y=3 brightest, y=4 a touch softer) reading as a sunlit surface ripple, and a single softer mid-water ripple (y=10). Each band spans the full width so every row stays constant in x -- the bands preserve the horizontal uniformity from the gradient, so the tile is still seamless left<->right. These bands are the moving content: when we shift the frame vertically they slide to new rows, which is what makes the animation visible.

Audit the finished base tile on the axis that matters. HORIZONTAL must report 0 mismatches: the gradient and bands are uniform in x, so column 15 == column 0 on every row -- side-by-side tiling is seamless by construction. We deliberately do NOT assert anything about the VERTICAL seam: this is a horizontal water strip (it repeats sideways only), so a top<->bottom join is irrelevant here -- the bright crest at the top is meant to abut the deep floor at the bottom, and tiling it vertically is simply not a thing we do. We test exactly the axis the tile is built to satisfy.
Frame 1 is an exact copy of frame 0, so the vertical wrap-shift below is the frame's only delta.

Roll frame 1 four pixels DOWN with wrap=true (dx=0). Because the content actually differs row-to-row (the crest and ripple bands), shifting along y genuinely relocates pixels -- frame 1 is NOT identical to frame 0, so the GIF will visibly animate. And shifting purely along y can never touch the horizontal seam: each row is still uniform across x after the shift (a row moved wholesale to a new y is still constant in x), so column 15 == column 0 everywhere and the left<->right tiling stays seamless. Vertical is the seamless-and-animatable axis for this strip.

Frame 2 also branches from the pristine frame 0 (not from frame 1), so its offset is absolute: a single +8px vertical shift instead of two stacked +4px shifts. Keeps the math exact and avoids compounding.
Frame 2 = +8px down. Twice the per-frame step keeps the apparent downward flow speed constant across the loop. The bands now sit half a tile lower than frame 0.
Frame 3 from frame 0 again, same absolute-offset reasoning.
Frame 3 = +12px down, the third quarter step. Frames 0..3 advance dy 0,4,8,12, so the crest and ripple bands sweep smoothly downward a quarter-tile each frame.
Frame 4, the explicit closing frame, also branches from pristine frame 0.

Frame 4 = +16px down. On a 16-tall tile a toroidal +16 shift is the identity (shift uses y.rem_euclid(16), and 16 mod 16 == 0), so frame 4 is pixel-IDENTICAL to frame 0 -- the bands have swept a full tile down and wrapped exactly back to where they started. This is the explicit closing frame that makes the loop literally close onto itself: dy goes 0,4,8,12,16==0, five evenly-spaced quarter-steps with the last landing back on the start. (The bands move on every step 0->1->2->3->4; only the final +16 returns to identity, by design.)

Verify a shifted frame on x. A vertical toroidal shift of a horizontally-uniform tile is STILL horizontally uniform (every row is just relocated, never broken across x), so frame 3 must ALSO report 0 horizontal mismatches -- direct proof the vertical wrap-shift kept the tile seamless left<->right, not just frame 0.

The animation proof. doc_frame_diff reports `changed` = added + removed + recolored pixels between frame 0 and frame 1. It MUST be > 0: the +4px vertical shift moved the crest and ripple bands to new rows, so many pixels recolour. This is the test the old horizontal-shift version would FAIL -- there every row was identical so a horizontal roll produced pixel-identical frames (changed == 0) and the GIF was a still image. changed > 0 here is what guarantees the loop genuinely animates.

The eyeball check: render frame 0 repeated in a 2x2 grid. A horizontally-seamless tile reads as one continuous body of water across the left<->right join with no visible vertical grid line; the horizontal join between stacked copies is intentionally visible (this tile only repeats sideways).

Tag frames 0..4 as a forward loop named 'flow'. The span includes the explicit closing frame 4 (the +16==0 identity), so the played sequence is 0,1,2,3,4 and its last frame is pixel-identical to its first -- which is what lets the loop-seam audit below read a true 0.0.

Loop-seam audit: it diffs the wrap the loop actually plays, last played frame -> first played frame. For tag 'flow' that is frame 4 -> frame 0. Because frame 4 is the +16==0 identity it is pixel-identical to frame 0, so changed == 0 and seam_score is 0.0 -- the shift cycle closes onto itself with no leftover offset and the loop restarts with no visible cut. Note the distinction from doc_frame_diff above: adjacent frames DIFFER (0->1 moved 256 px, the animation), yet the LOOP as a whole closes seamlessly because its endpoints coincide. (We made the closing frame explicit -- frame 4 -- rather than relying on an implicit wrap step, because this audit literally diffs the last and first frames of the played sequence; it has no knowledge of the per-frame shift, so the cycle must be closed by an actual frame whose pixels match frame 0.)

Export the 'flow' loop as an 8x GIF for the final visual check: the wave bands should visibly drift downward frame to frame and wrap smoothly. NOTE: out_path is relative to your working directory; point it somewhere outside the repo (or delete it after) so the example doesn't leave a build artifact behind.
